acts.title: Describing the chart in words
text: The number of one-person households ___ steadily from 1970 to about 2005.
It then ___ at just under thirty per cent and stopped climbing.
Between 2005 and 2012 the line ___, moving by less than one point in either direction.

tts: Conversation one. I hope you don’t mind me asking, but haven’t we met somewhere before? — I’m not sure, you do look familiar. — Are you a friend of Nicola’s? — Yes, we went to school together. — Ah, so did I. What class were you in?

Conversation two. Sorry, but I couldn’t help overhearing — it’s your first day today, isn’t it? — Yes, I’m Peter’s new personal assistant. — Ah. Welcome to the firm. I’m Josie, I work in Sales. — Good to meet you. I’m Sita.

Conversation three. Excuse me, is anyone sitting there? — No, go ahead. — Is it always this busy? — Yes, I’m afraid so. You don’t usually take this one, then? — No, I’ve just started a new job in the city.

items.q: Where does the second conversation take place?
o: At work, on somebody’s first day

items.q: How does the third speaker open the conversation?
o: By asking whether a seat is free

items.q: What do all three openings have in common?
o: They begin with an apology or a soft question, not a statement
They are all about the weather

acts.title: Communal Living
tts: San Francisco is one of the fastest-growing cities in the USA. Thanks to its location just north of Silicon Valley, business is booming and the city is attracting some of the world’s most successful technology companies.
But traditionally San Francisco has always felt more like a small city than a bustling metropolis. In the sixties and seventies it was a vibrant hub of art, music and politics.

Today the city’s writers and activists live alongside technology entrepreneurs and millionaire business leaders. This has created a new buzz, but some feel San Francisco is losing its sense of community. One reason is house prices: the city now has the most expensive average house prices of any American city, and many long-time residents are moving to more affordable locations just outside.

This is Sausalito, a small waterfront community just across the Golden Gate Bridge. A large number of residents here still work in the city but prefer the small-town feel. However, thanks to the influx of new residents, house prices here are rising too, with the average Sausalito house costing more than one million dollars.

But one area still offers affordable housing and a strong neighbourly spirit: Sausalito’s houseboat community. Right on the dock of Richardson Bay there are four hundred floating homes across five marinas.

items.q: What has changed in San Francisco?
o: House prices have risen and long-time residents are leaving

items.q: Why do people move to Sausalito?
o: For the small-town feel, while still working in the city
Because it is closer to the airport

items.q: What is unusual about the houseboat community?
o: It is still affordable and has a strong neighbourly spirit
It is the most expensive area

acts.title: Communal Living
tts: There are four hundred floating homes across five purpose-built marinas on Richardson Bay.
One resident has lived there for forty-one years, since 1974, and says he has never lived anywhere else this long. Another moved in 1997 and has therefore been there eighteen years.
During the Second World War the area was home to a huge industrial shipyard, which closed in 1945. Immediately afterwards a number of people moved there and converted the old boats into homes.
The average Sausalito house costs more than one million dollars, while the houseboats remain comparatively affordable.
The houseboat owners face constant maintenance, so residents work together, sharing knowledge, tools and labour.

acts.title: Two jobs: opening a conversation, and describing a chart
rule: These look unrelated and are not. Both are about approaching something carefully. An opening line that is too direct makes a stranger uncomfortable; a description of data that is too direct — just reading the numbers aloud — tells the reader nothing they could not see.
points: Apologize first, then ask. I hope you don’t mind me asking… Sorry, I couldn’t help overhearing…
After mind, use the -ing form: do you mind me asking, would you mind waiting.
Name the movement, then the size, then the period. The figure rose sharply between 2000 and 2005.
A good description says what is noticeable, not what every number is. The most noticeable feature is…
roughly, just under, approximately, around. Exact figures in prose read as false precision.
eg: I hope you don’t mind me asking, but haven’t we met before?
Apologize, then ask.
Sorry, I couldn’t help overhearing.
The standard way into somebody else’s conversation.
Excuse me, is anyone sitting there?
A question, not a statement — it gives them an exit.
Would you mind waiting a moment?
mind + -ing.
The figure rose sharply between 2000 and 2005.
Movement, size, period.
It then levelled off at just under thirty per cent.
level off + at.
Numbers peaked in 2005 and fell slightly after that.
peak, then fall.
The most noticeable feature of the data is the gap between age groups.
What to open a description with.
Roughly a third of households now contain one person.
Hedged, and easier to read than 32.7 per cent.
Most of the growth has come from outside Europe.
RECYCLED: most of the, for a defined group.
acts.careful: “Do you mind to ask?” and “I couldn’t help to overhear” are both wrong. Both structures take the -ing form.

write.q: Describe, in about 180 words, a change in how people live where you are — household size, who lives with whom, how long people stay in one home. You do not need real statistics; use the figures you believe to be roughly right and hedge them properly. Open with what is most noticeable, describe the movement rather than listing numbers, and finish with what you think explains it.
plan: how the figure moved, and when
one thing that has stayed the same
write.model:
The most noticeable feature of household size in Karaganda over the last thirty years is how little it has changed compared with almost everywhere else.

The average household fell steadily through the 1990s, from roughly four and a half people to something just under four, and most of that fall came from families leaving the country altogether rather than from young people setting up alone. It then levelled off, and it has stayed at about the same figure ever since.

What has not changed at all is the proportion of homes containing three generations. Roughly a third of the flats in my own block do, which is close to what it was when I was at school.

The explanation is not cultural, whatever visitors assume. It is childcare and rent, in that order. Very few of the people I know who live with their parents have chosen it for the reason strangers guess.
